tnca.device: AMD/Xilinx Alveo U280 (xcu280), FPGA prototype image
tnca.power_note: no power measurement in the TNCA records; board power not measured

spec.source: archbench/specs/gpu_gb10.json (spec_peak facts used by the ArchBench GPU bound)

gpu.clocks: not locked (no root); the SM clock observed during sustained loops is in each boundary record

power_w.note: nvidia-smi power.draw as the driver reports it for GB10 (not wall power, not the whole system); sustained = back-to-back resident calls of one point for >= 2 s, sampled every ~0.1 s (small points are host-bound and barely load the GPU); snapshot = one reading when an ArchBench record starts, before its warm-up, with the device between points

boundaries.name: makespan
boundaries.tnca_definition: first accepted launch to last device completion (sequence-checked MMIO endpoints); host submission gaps and backpressure included; no cache flush, after one untimed warm-up call
boundaries.gpu_definition: first CUDA device activity start to last device activity end of one call (CUPTI via torch.profiler); launch/scheduling gaps included; no flush, after 3 warm-up calls
differences: GPU timestamps come from CUPTI with the profiler active, which can lengthen host launch gaps of the non-graph variants; TNCA endpoints are device-clock MMIO counters
TNCA: one timed sample per point (functional inventory sampling); GPU: median of 10-25 profiled calls

boundaries.name: serial-sum
boundaries.tnca_definition: sum over the call's launches of launch-accept-to-core-idle cycles; gaps excluded
boundaries.gpu_definition: sum of the call's device activity durations (kernels, memsets, copies); gaps excluded; no flush
differences: a GPU kernel duration is its own makespan over the SMs; a TNCA launch ROI is the launch makespan over the 3 cores

boundaries.name: resident-call
boundaries.tnca: timings["resident-call-latency"] median, or on the native resident path timings["request-latency"] median (0 bytes uploaded or downloaded: inputs and module resident, outputs left on the device)
boundaries.tnca_definition: host time.monotonic() from the call until the graph is complete
boundaries.gpu_definition: host time.monotonic() around fn(*inputs) and torch.cuda.synchronize(); module and inputs resident (.cuda()), outputs left on the device; no flush
differences: TNCA: one sample per point; GPU: median of 20-50 calls
host CPUs differ (TNCA: acf3019 x86_64 over PCIe MMIO; GPU: GB10 Arm cores, unified memory)

boundaries.name: request
boundaries.tnca: not in the native-path records (request-latency there is the resident call)
boundaries.gpu_definition: in-place host-to-device copy of every input, the call, .cpu() of every output
differences: no TNCA counterpart in these records; GPU figure reported for completeness

boundaries.name: archbench-gpu-primary
boundaries.tnca: (none paired) TNCA device-cycles-serial-grid is the nearest kind
boundaries.gpu: archbench time.device (CUPTI activity sum, L2 + system cache flushed before the call), time.latency_cold / latency_warm (CUDA events around the call)
differences: cold cache on the GPU, no flush on TNCA
CUDA-event latency is device-side and includes the host time before the first launch; TNCA has no event-based figure
reported unchanged as the primary ArchBench GPU record and as a cross-check of the boundary harness (cupti-sum-cold should agree with it)

caveats: Different resource and power scope: TNCA is a 3-core FPGA prototype at 90 MHz on a U280 card (an FPGA-fabric-limited clock); the GPU is a 48-SM GB10 at up to 3 GHz sharing LPDDR5X with its CPU. Time ratios here compare these two systems as built; they are not normalised by area, clock, power or process and do not predict an ASIC.
No commercial-ASIC figures are used or compared (R40-10 acceptance 4).

TNCA sampling is the functional inventory plan: one untimed warm-up call and one timed call per point. Device-cycle kinds are deterministic within 0.2 % on this board (v3 change 5); the host resident-call latency is a single sample and carries host noise.

Warm vs cold: TNCA timed calls follow one warm-up with no cache flush, so the paired GPU figures are the warm (no-flush) ones. ArchBench's primary GPU device time is cold-L2 and is reported beside them, not paired.

The TNCA makespan includes host submission gaps between launches (MMIO dispatch per launch); gap_fraction = 1 - serial-sum/makespan shows how much of each makespan they are. Under inductor-cudagraph the GPU replays the whole call as one CUDA graph; under the Triton variants kernels are launched one by one from Python and their host gaps enter the GPU span the same way.

Precision is the point's dtype on both sides (FP16 with FP32 accumulation on tensor cores / MMA; FP32 points in IEEE binary32, TF32 off) and both are checked against the same FP32 reference and tolerance.

inductor-triton as ArchBench freezes it (max_autotune_gemm with backends=TRITON) has no GEMM choice on GB10: Inductor disables Triton GEMM templates below 68 SMs (is_big_gpu), so its GEMM points fail with NoValidChoicesError. These failures are kept. inductor-triton-bigsm is the same configuration with that check forced true, a supplementary variant from tools/r40/v3_gpu_boundaries.py, not an ArchBench variant.

"Triton-only" covers GEMMs: in the Triton variants Inductor still lowers some operators to library kernels (e.g. SDPA to flash attention, convolution to cuDNN); kernel_classes and triton_only in each boundary row list what ran.
GPU clocks are not locked and the GPU is shared; the SM clock and power during the sustained loop and the nvidia-smi state at each record start are kept in the raw records.

GPU kernels of the small tiers run for about 1-10 µs; the same point measured in separate processes (ArchBench cold sum vs the boundary harness cold sum) differs by a factor 0.77-1.46, so per-point GPU figures at that scale carry that spread.
